title: The Vale of Ash
intro: The barrow on the hill has opened, and a gray blight creeps down the vale. Someone must go up and bind the Hollow King within to rest — only one path is needed: find the 3 verses — drowned shrine, old watchtower, barrow's own walls — or win his crown back from the elder's guarded coffer, proof of his grief in hand. Either alone rests him; both together just rests him deeper. It kills slow: no clock runs against you. The notice board in the square lays out the rest.
objectives: Either path ends this: speak the three stone verses — one in the drowned shrine, one atop the old watchtower (both east of the wood), one cut into the barrow's own walls — or win the king's crown back from the elder's guarded coffer, its iron band holding a fourth verse of its own — the elder won't yield it until you've heard the king's own grief at the throne first and carried proof back down — or both together, for a deeper rest. Four verses exist in all, three in stone and one in iron, but no single path needs all four. Sealing the barrow after is separate, arranged with the reeve or priest at the throne. Kneeling there instead of finishing either path ends your story at once, with no dawn to come. Speak to the same folk more than once, too — a second word from them often runs deeper than the first. The verse tally updates the instant you find one — trust the number shown, no need to recount by hand.

East, a hungry wolf prowls the trail before the drowned shrine and watchtower beyond — the barrow trail north runs calmer. West, past the bridge, woodsmoke marks a hunter's camp — herbs and a barrow way in.

gate.name: Village Gate
gate.desc: The last gate before the wood. Lanterns burn all day here now. Two roads lead to the barrow, either enough alone: the old verses or the king's crown. Worth a stop south in the square first, before the trail — the smith has steel to spare, the inn a bed, the elder the king's crown behind a locked coffer, and the gray priest a blessing that alone unlocks the barrow doors, no force or luck required. The notice board there explains: the reeve wants the barrow sealed once the Hollow King rests, the gray priest wants it opened instead, still grieving him — a separate choice, yours to make either road. The Ashwood waits north: keep straight on for the barrow trail, the crown road; bear east once inside for the drowned shrine and, further north of it, the old watchtower, the verse road; a hunter's camp lies west of that.

square.name: Last Light Square
square.desc: Packed earth and a dry well. The reeve stands watch by a notice board — the short of it, verses or crown, either alone ends this; read the board for the rest. Inn west, forge east, chapel south.

actions.label: read the notice board
fx: Notice board: the dead king in the barrow won't rest — folk here call him the Hollow King. Worth a stop before the trail: the forge east fits a free blade, no charge; the inn west keeps a wandering scholar and a warm bed. Two ways to settle him — walk either alone, or both for a deeper rest: the old verses, one in the drowned shrine, one atop the old watchtower, one in the barrow's own walls, each cut into stone and traced by touch as readily as read, all three needed. Or his crown, old iron rumored to bear a verse of its own inside the band, sealed in the village elder's coffer east past the chapel. The crown itself won't come free without proof of his grief — hear him grieve yourself, up at the throne; his seal, carried back, can back your word after, but never stands in for hearing it firsthand. Mind — this is the tale's one trap, not a fourth path: kneel before him without verse or crown in hand, and you take his place instead. The game ends right there, no dawn, nothing after. The barrow's side rooms hold plunder too, no bearing on how it ends: a mail shirt in its crypt for armor, a locked strongbox with the king's seal that can ease the crown road later — and a real place, not just talk, the hunter's camp west in the ashwood, past the bridge: herbs to trade and a hidden way into the barrow, same plunder terms. Separately: the reeve wants the barrow sealed shut for good after; the gray priest, in the chapel south past the well, wants it opened instead — he remembers the old king's grief and thinks the dead deserve better than a stone lid — ask him and he'll open the barrow doors himself, no forcing required. Mind — the two can't both be courted: promise the reeve and the priest's own blessing closes to you unless he later frees you from that word, which costs the reeve's trust in turn. Which doors you leave sealed or open at the end is still your choice alone, made last, at the throne, when the tale ends.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: More, in a finer hand: one path is the old verses. Three lie in the drowned shrine, the old watchtower — through the gate, then east into the ash wood (get your bearings once you're among the trees) — and the barrow's own walls; speak all three together at the throne. The other path is the king's crown, sealed in the village elder's coffer — though the elder won't yield it until you've heard the old king's own grief at the throne first, then carried the proof back down; the crown road circles through the barrow twice where the verses need it once. Water, wind, stone, and the crown besides — all four carry the same old refrain, each closing the same way: '...and rest.'

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: Another hand added: the crown was taken from him long ago, by his own kin no less — the reason his rest won't come. Hear his grief at the throne first, then press the elder for it.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: A last line, added later: either path ends it alone, though the two together leave nothing unresolved. Mind — the verses read quick only for a scholar's eye, or come clear at a touch for quiet, quick hands; anyone else puzzles them out slow, deep in the wood, three sites over — no one site harder than the others, nothing cursed about any of them, same trick wherever it's cut — or asks the wandering scholar warming their hands at the inn west for the trick of it. The crown is the steadier road if that's not your gift — one lock in the vault for the seal, then the elder to convince. Steadier, but slighter: three hard-won verses are remembered better than one quick coffer, and the vale honors the difference.

elder_house.name: Elder's House

onEnterOnce: "That coffer," the elder says, following your eyes to it, "opens for one proof — you, having heard the old king grieve for himself, up in the barrow. That's required, no way round it. His seal isn't: carry it and it'll back your word, sparing you the trouble of convincing me — but alone, it opens nothing."

barrow_field.name: Barrow Field
barrow_field.desc: A bare hill and two stone doors set into it, facing north. The grass here is white, not gray. You notice a loose stone by the ivy, gapped from its neighbors.

north.lockedMsg: The stone doors are shut fast. Try what's in front of you, or find the gray priest at the chapel south of the square for a blessing — none of it's certain to work.
north.hint: the gray priest at the chapel south of the square, for a blessing — or try what's below

actions.label: get your bearings
fx: From the hilltop you can see it plain: the village lies south down the trail, and past the wood to the east stand the drowned shrine and the old watchtower. First time out, that means back down to the gate, then north into the wood and east from there. Once you've stood in either, though, the village square keeps its own quick trail straight back — no need to walk the wood twice.

antechamber.name: Barrow Antechamber

Two optional side trips branch off here: east, an iron-strapped door hides a locked strongbox — force or pick it for the king's seal, armor and a shortcut past the elder's doubt. Down, a crypt holds a mail shirt, armor enough to blunt every blow after. Neither is needed for any ending. (A * on an exit below marks one of these, unexplored.)
antechamber.brief: Empty niches — the doors' fate, seal or open, still waits at the throne. East, the strongbox may hold the king's seal, proof for the elder; down, the crypt may hold armor. (A * below marks an unexplored side path — optional, nothing the ending needs.)
onEnterOnce: These niches once held tokens for the dead. He will not come for you unprovoked — mind what was warned outside. Whatever you settle with him ahead will also seal these doors shut or leave them open behind you.

vault.name: The King's Strongroom
vault.desc: A side chamber the wight never had to guard — the old king trusted iron more than claws. A strongbox sits under years of dust, its lock long rusted, and in the corner a robed shade sits so still you take it for shadow until it speaks. The antechamber lies west.

onEnterOnce: Whatever this held, no one has touched it in a long time — the old king's seal, if it's still inside, could ease your case with the elder later on the crown road, and like the mail shirt in the crypt, it counts as light armor too: no need to wear it, just carrying it blunts blows from here on. Nothing here is needed to finish the tale, and losing it costs nothing else — skip it if you'd rather press on than spend the turns. The lock looks temperamental, but iron doesn't wear out from trying — safe to force or pick as many times as you like.

actions.label: force the strongbox — safe to try as many times as you like

crypt.name: Barrow Crypt
crypt.desc: Low vaults and stone boxes, the air gone sour and the mold black instead of green — whatever is killing the fields above pools thickest right here. Fighting it isn't required — go up and reach the throne through the hall of verses instead, if you'd rather not.

The same blight pooling in the fields above runs thickest right here — no shame taking iron against it, no need to wear it either, it wards off blows riding in your pack. The wight ahead: beat it for its relic and the way north, slip by instead if quiet's your way (scout), or skip it clean — the hall of verses reaches the throne just as well, no cost to leaving it be.

throne.name: Throne of the Barrow
throne.desc: The Hollow King sits on a stone seat, worn smooth by hands not his own. Where a crown should be, there is only dust. Cold air gutters your light as you cross the threshold. South: crypt. Down: hall of verses.

The reeve, back in the square, wants the doors sealed once he rests — give your word early and keep it, and the watch trusts you further; break it and word travels the other way. The gray priest, in the chapel, wants them left open for the grief to breathe, and his own blessing can open them for you first. The village elder, past the chapel, holds the old king's crown, if you'd rather settle him with it instead of verses — though the elder won't yield it until you've heard his grief yourself, same as you're hearing it now. None of the three is required — walk out and decide alone if you'd rather, and it costs you nothing you haven't already spent.

By harvest the orchard rows hang heavy with fruit no one expected this year, and the vale keeps a bowl of grain by the sealed door out of a habit nobody can quite explain.

actions.label: (ends it now, the deeper rest) return the crown and speak the three verses, breaking your word to the reeve and leaving the barrow open
fx: You set the crown in his hands and speak the three verses over him, all at once. He listens through them with the crown finally where it belongs, and something in his face settles the rest of the way. The gray lifts from the vale by morning and does not come back. You gave the reeve your word the doors would seal — and you don't keep it; the barrow doors stand open behind you all the same. He takes the broken oath harder than silence would have cost you; the gray priest, at least, is glad of it. By harvest the orchard rows hang heavy with fruit no one expected this year, and the vale keeps a bowl of grain on the barrow steps out of a habit nobody can quite explain.

actions.label: (ends it now, the deeper rest) return the crown and speak the three verses, sealing the barrow after, though you never promised to
fx: You set the crown in his hands and speak the three verses over him, all at once. He listens through them with the crown finally where it belongs, and something in his face settles the rest of the way. The gray lifts from the vale by morning and does not come back. No one asked it of you, but you seal the doors shut behind you anyway — the reeve takes the news gladly enough; the gray priest still would rather they'd stood open. By harvest the orchard rows hang heavy with fruit no one expected this year, and the vale keeps a bowl of grain by the sealed door out of a habit nobody can quite explain.

actions.label: (ends your story, no dawn) kneel and become the vale's new hollow king
fx: You kneel. The crown of nothing settles on you, light as ash. The vale will have a king after all — and no dawn. No promise of yours seals this place; none is needed now.

fx: You kneel. The crown of nothing settles on you, light as ash. The vale will have a king after all — and no dawn. The seal you promised the reeve no longer matters — you are what the doors would have kept in.

actions.label: (ends it now, a bad end) pocket the crown and leave him unrested, grieving
fx: You pocket the crown and turn for the stairs, leaving him exactly as you found him — no verse spoken, nothing returned, nothing settled. He doesn't call after you. Back on the surface the gray does not lift; it thickens by the week, crops failing further, the well running low, the vale still waiting on a dawn you never bring. Somewhere below, he's still sitting on that stone seat, and he will go on sitting there long after you've left the vale for good.

topics.label: the blight
topics.say: It kills slow. Crops first, then cattle, then the will to stay. It started the night the barrow opened. Two roads end it: verses, or crown. Ask about the barrow — seal or open — if you mean to see this through.

topics.label: the barrow
topics.say: Here's the choice, plain: seal the barrow once he rests, or leave it open — that's yours to make, not mine. I want it sealed — the gray priest wants it left open, that's the whole of our quarrel. Settled later, at the throne, whatever you say now. Give me your word today, though, and the priest's own blessing for these doors closes with it. Change your mind after, and he can free you from that word — it costs my trust, not his. My trust alone is a small thing — keep faith or break it, and you'll only hear it in what we each say to you later. The promise itself is not small: it decides whether those doors stand open or seal for good, and the tale told after remembers which one you chose. No rush: promise now or before you reach the throne, and saying no plain costs you nothing. Words serve as well as verses, if you'd rather press the elder for the old king's crown, east past the chapel. One more thing, plain: stand before him without verse or crown and kneel anyway, and you take his place — no dawn after. Don't kneel empty-handed.

topics.label: the two roads
topics.say: Two ways up that hill, if you want it plain. The old words are cut in stone — shrine, tower, barrow wall, three of them — read a verse in the old tongue or trace it by hand, and you needn't chase the other one at all. Or there's his crown, locked in the elder's coffer, though the elder wants proof of his grief before it opens. Either road ends this alone. Walk both, if your legs hold out, and he rests deeper for it.

topics.label: which road suits me
topics.say: The wood won't hand the verses over at a glance — not unless the old tongue comes easy to you, or you've a scholar's ear at the inn to teach you the trick of it. The crown road's steadier for the rest of us: one lock to spring, then the elder's patience to wear down. Steadier, but slighter — the vale remembers three hard verses longer than one quick key.

topics.label: promise to seal the barrow (closes off the priest's blessing)
topics.say: Good. The watch stands with you now, and it pleases me. I'm holding you to seal these doors once the king rests, however you settle him, crown or verse or both — the choosing happens there, not here, but I'll remember whether you kept your word. The gray priest's blessing is closed to you from here, unless he frees you from the word himself. Change your mind later, and it's him you'd have to ask, not me. Reeve's trust: gained.

topics.label: decline to promise
topics.say: Then say so plain, and I'll hold nothing against you for it. The doors stay open when the king rests — no promise made, none broken. Ask again before you're done, if you change your mind.

topics.label: is there a compromise?
topics.say: No, truly — seal or leave it open is the whole choice, same as I said. There's no third way now, only a way back out later: promise if you're leaning that way, and the gray priest, south of here in the chapel, will free you from the word whenever you ask after — same cost to my trust as always.

topics.label: the watch's aid
topics.say: Then take the watch shield. It has stopped worse than claws.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open, for now. That's the king's doing, not yours breaking your word — the promise still holds. Seal them once he rests, same as you told me, and the watch won't forget it either way.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: So they're open. No promise of yours says they close again after — I told you I wouldn't count silence as one, and I meant it. Doesn't mean I've stopped hoping.

topics.label: the priest's release
topics.say: He said as much himself, then, in his own way — no need to spell it out further. I'd rather have heard it from you first, but I'll take it plain over hearing it from no one. Doesn't undo the asking. Just means I know where I stand with you now. He asks for the shield back, too — the watch's, not yours to keep on a broken word. You hand it over.

topics.label: the priest's release
topics.say: He said as much himself, then, in his own way — no need to spell it out further. I'd rather have heard it from you first, but I'll take it plain over hearing it from no one. Doesn't undo the asking. Just means I know where I stand with you now.

topics.label: the scrap of cloth
topics.say: The reeve turns it over, and the color goes out of their face. "Watch gray. Fine-woven — a reeve's cloth, not a common one's." A long pause. "There was a reeve before me, generations back, who went up to the barrow alone and never came down the same road. Records say he took something that wasn't his to take. We always thought the wood took him for it." They hand it back. "Bury it proper, if you pass that way again. He's earned that much."

topics.label: what the watch says about you now
topics.say: You'll have noticed the watch stopped stopping you at the gate. Word travels fast in a square this small — say a thing and keep it, and it follows you the rest of the way through.

topics.label: what the watch says about you now
topics.say: You'll have noticed the watch holds you longer at the gate these days, and asks more of you than they used to. Word travels fast in a square this small — break a thing you swore to keep, or leave a door open against my hope, and it follows you the rest of the way through, same as keeping one would have.

topics.label: you know I've been to the chapel
topics.say: Word travels fast in a square this small — I heard you'd found the chapel before you came back to me. He'll have told you grief needs open air. I still say it needs a shut door. Hear us both out if you must, but don't make a habit of it — a promise means less to me the longer you keep the two of us guessing.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say. One in the drowned shrine east of the wood, one up the old watchtower north of that, one cut into the barrow stone itself. A scholar's eye reads them quick — anyone else will have to puzzle them out slow. Some skip the puzzle and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Word is the elder holds something taken from the old king himself; a silver tongue might settle that debt quicker than any verse. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Quiet hands can trace any of the three by touch, if grace holds, same as they find their own ways in where doors won't open — no scholar's eye needed at any of them. Some skip the puzzle altogether and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Whatever's down there, plenty would rather you just settle it with steel. Others skip the verses entirely and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: the reeve and the gray priest
topics.say: Those two haven't agreed on a thing in years. The reeve wants the barrow shut for good once the king's settled; the priest wants it left open, still grieving him — and it's the priest's own blessing that can open those doors for you now, if you'd rather not force them. Promise the reeve first, though, and that blessing closes with it. Ask either one plain and you'll hear the same split — you can't promise both.

topics.label: the inn's regulars
topics.say: Even the reeve's watch drink here on their nights off — you'd be surprised what loosens over a second cup. Ask around long enough and half the vale's secrets end up on this counter, one way or another.

topics.label: about the old tongue
topics.say: You've the trick already — a scholar's eye reads these stones outright, no tip of mine needed there. Still, carry it with you: a sharper mind serves wherever else you must puzzle a way through by wits alone.

topics.label: ask about the one line that beat her
topics.say: 'Every scholar meets one line that won't sit still,' she says, testing you. 'Care to try the one that beat me?'
fx: The line gives before you've even sat down — faster than she managed, by her own account. 'Keep that ease,' she says. 'The barrow won't be as patient as I was.'
The line won't sit still for you either, not this time. 'Good,' she says, not unkindly. 'Means you're still reading, not just remembering.'

topics.label: about the old tongue
topics.say: I've spent years on stones like these. Watch how the marks repeat, and the pattern starts to show. Carry that with you — it should ease any verse you find out there.

topics.label: the old king
topics.say: He was a good king, long ago, and he was robbed of his crown in his own grave — the vale calls him the Hollow King now. Sealed in stone, grief festers; open sky lets it go. Ask me for a blessing and I will open the barrow doors myself. The reeve wants them shut — you decide, at the throne, once he finally rests. His crown sits in the elder's coffer besides — that opens for proof of the same grief: hear him grieve for himself, up in the barrow, first and always.

topics.label: the old king
topics.say: He was a good king, long ago, and he was robbed of his crown in his own grave — the vale calls him the Hollow King now. Sealed in stone, grief like that festers; open sky lets it go. You have already given the reeve your word, though — I will not offer what undoes it. The doors must open some other way now. His crown still sits in the elder's coffer besides, if you'd have it — that opens for proof of the same grief: hear him grieve for himself, up in the barrow, first and always. His seal, if the barrow still holds one, can back your word after — but won't stand in for hearing him.

topics.label: a blessing for the barrow
topics.say: Go with the gray blessing, then. Far off, the stone doors glow and creak open, unsealed — no promise binds them shut. Go whenever you're ready.

topics.label: release from your promise
topics.say: Vows are not mine to unmake, only to witness broken. I'll say nothing to the reeve of it — but you will have to, in the end. Go with a clear path, if not a clear conscience. Reeve's trust: lost. Priest's trust: gained. Keep this steadiness, too — it'll serve you again, next time your nerve is the only thing standing between you and what you came for.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open now, sealed later — the reeve's word, not mine. I'll not pretend that pleases me. A door is a poor answer to grief, whichever side of it stays shut.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open, and no promise waiting to shut them again. Good. Let him have his air, whatever comes of him after.

topics.label: the verses you carry
topics.say: So the old words are opening to you after all, and you never needed my blessing for it. Good — the king rests either way, and the reeve gets his sealed doors regardless of what I think of them. I'd rather he'd never asked you first, but I'll not begrudge you the verses for it.

topics.label: what the priest says about you now
topics.say: You come back to this chapel more than most do. I don't mistake that for faith — but I've stopped bracing for an argument each time you do.

topics.label: you know I've spoken to the reeve
topics.say: Word travels faster than grief, in a square this small. I don't fault you for hearing him out — only for thinking there's a way to keep both of us pleased. There isn't, in the end. Ash and mud don't share a hearth.

topics.label: the ash on his hands
topics.say: Every barrow I've opened leaves its mark. This one, before you're done, likely will too — on you as well as me, whichever road you take to it.

topics.label: steel for the barrow
topics.say: Take the plain sword — and hold still, I'll put a working edge on whatever you carry. If it's the crown you're after, the elder keeps it — coffer's locked, east past the chapel.

topics.label: the smith's trade
topics.say: Every blade in this square passed through my hands, or my mother's before me. None of them come back from that wood the same. Still, they come back.

topics.label: why she watches the road
topics.say: Every set of shoulders coming out of that wood tells me something before they open their mouth. I've learned to read it. Doesn't mean I like what it says most days.

topics.label: the old king's steel
topics.say: So the priest's told you about him. My grandmother swore the old king's own blade was never found in that barrow — maybe that's why he lingers. Or maybe that's just an old smith's tale, passed down for the telling.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Word beat you back to the square — the barrow stands open. I've fitted edges for that wood my whole life and never once expected the doors to be the thing that finally gave.

topics.label: the vale
topics.say: Four hundred years this village has kept the wood's edge. It will not end on my page of the ledger.

topics.label: the elder's years
topics.say: I've buried two reeves and outlasted three bad harvests in this chair. The wood took my brother, years before any king lost his crown. I don't forget what it takes.

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "Proof," the elder says. "His grievance, in his own words, or something bearing his mark. You have neither yet."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You have the king's own seal," the elder says, "but not his grievance. Words carry more weight with me than metal."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You've heard his grief," the elder says. "The king's own seal would settle it outright — but your word alone may yet be enough."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You have both," the elder says. "His grievance, and the king's own seal to back it. Nothing holds this coffer shut now but my own doubt."

topics.label: the king's stolen crown
topics.say: You tell the elder what the old king grieves for: his crown, taken from the barrow. "I know," the elder says. "Bring me proof of that grief — his own words, or his seal — and the coffer opens."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You ask about the coffer. The elder's hand covers the ledger. "That's not open to asking — not from you, not yet. Go hear what the dead king himself grieves over, up in the barrow. His seal, if a strongbox there still holds it, would prove it outright, but even without it, come back and tell me what he grieves over. That may be reason enough."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You set the king's seal on the table between you. The elder's hand stills on the ledger — recognition, not surprise. "That mark is real. I know it." But their grip doesn't loosen. "Metal doesn't settle what's between him and me. Go hear what he grieves over yourself, up in the barrow — then come back and we'll speak of the coffer."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: No lock holds this shut, only the elder's own doubt. You press the old king's grievance on them, your word against their will, and the elder's hands close on the ledger.
fx: Your silver tongue finds the old argument the elder has been having with themself, and settles it. The coffer creaks open. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You set the king's own seal on the ledger, his hand plain in the scrap beneath it — proof no words could match. The elder's doubt has nowhere left to stand.
fx: The coffer opens without another word. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: No lock holds this shut, only the elder's own doubt. You press the old king's grievance on them, your word against their will, and the elder's hands close on the ledger.
fx: At last your will outlasts the elder's. Their hands unclench, and they open the coffer. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

The elder's resolve holds, this time. Ask again, the same question, and press harder — the coffer will give eventually. Or leave it: the barrow verses reach the same end without the crown, deeper together.

The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

topics.label: read the crown's band before you decide
fx: Turning the iron over, you find words worked into the inside of the band, worn thin but legible — the same plea cut into stone, water, and wind elsewhere in the vale, each closing the same way: 'Let the crown remember whose grief it bore; lay it down, and rest.' Iron makes one more — not required; the three cut verses and the crown already finish the rite, this just says why.

topics.label: the wood
topics.say: Wolves gone gray and wrong. Keep moving and keep iron close.

topics.label: trade for herbs
topics.say: Take them. Wolves run this wood, and worse waits under the hill — keep something for your wounds. Pay me by ending this.

topics.label: the green hollow you found
topics.say: That hollow east of here? Only green in the whole gray wood. I mark it every season, in case mine ever run dry. Good you took some — you'll want it before this is done.

topics.label: the old barrow
topics.say: Doors face north, sealed since before me. But roots and old rain hollowed the hill's flank some seasons back — a gap under a fallen stone, if the doors ever give you trouble. Talk is there's a locked strongbox in there too, and a crypt with an old suit of mail — real armor, both of them, worth the trouble if you can crack the lock or reach the crypt. Neither counts as a verse — the mail's just armor, the seal only eases the crown road if you walk it. Neither stands between you and the throne, or how it ends.

ash_wolf.name: ash wolf
onDeath: The wolf drops. Its gray coat goes to dust — the same gray spreading over the fields since the barrow opened.

gaunt_wolf.name: gaunt wolf
onDeath: The gaunt wolf falls still, ribs plain through the gray coat. Whatever's starving it started the night the barrow opened, same as the rest.

lean_wolf.name: lean wolf
onDeath: The lean wolf goes still, the last of the pack that watched the trail. Whatever's left of the gray thins with it.

cairn_husk.name: gray husk
onDeath: The husk crumbles to gray dust over the stones. Whatever held it together came apart the same night the barrow opened.

barrow_wight.name: barrow-wight
onDeath: The wight comes apart into rag and bone — and among the scraps, a ward-token of cold iron, the kind hung over a door to keep grief from walking in. Whatever it stood that long, stubborn watch to guard, slipping past would have left buried with it. The passage north stands open now.

hollow_king.name: hollow king

topics.label: why do you grieve
topics.say: My crown. The first reeve took it from my barrow, and my rest went with it — the elder keeps it sealed — now you have proof. Bring it back or speak the old verses — either rests me, each its own ending, both together deeper. Break it, or end me by the blade. Or kneel and take the crown for your own — that ends your story, no dawn for you. Only one road is yours to walk.

topics.label: the blight
topics.say: It is my grief, spilled over the land. It will not stop while I wake. Ask why I grieve, if you want the whole of it.

topics.label: memories
topics.say: Faces, mostly, and a good harvest the year they crowned me. This mound was already cut into the hill by then. The first reeve did not take my crown out of malice — he was my own blood, and the vale was cold and starving that winter; a dead king's gold bought more grain than a living king's promises ever had. I remember losing the crown far more clearly than wearing it.

topics.label: you may soon rest
topics.say: He lifts his head, though you have spoken nothing yet. "Three," he says, quiet. "Water for grief my own hands couldn't lay down, wind for what iron never carried off, stone for what my flesh forgot — three hands, laying the same weight down. I felt each one settle into the stone as you found it. Say them here, when you're ready, and let this be over."

topics.label: the sealed doors
topics.say: Sealed or open, it is no longer mine to keep. The reeve fears what walks free; the priest fears a shut door on grief undone. Both are half right. Leave it however you see fit — I will not haunt it either way.

onDeath: Your blade finds him and he breaks apart into dust and old iron, a king who never got his crown back. The blight dies with him — the gray thins out of the trees by morning. The vale will not know why. Only that the light came back. By spring, wildflowers crowd the barrow mound, and children dare each other to touch the door that used to keep them awake at night. The doors stand open behind you still — no one comes down to seal them, and whatever you told the reeve about it goes unasked and unanswered.

topics.label: who kept this room
topics.say: Forty years I held this key, and the king's trust with it. I do not haunt the box — only what it meant, that a man's word once needed iron behind it to be believed at all.

topics.label: the seal you broke
topics.say: His own blood pried the crown loose that same week — I heard both locks give, his and mine, one after the other. I kept faith with the wrong door.
